# The MeshTransformer stack: the mathematics {#sec-mesh-attention}

@sec-architecture says what the MeshTransformer *is* in plain language.
This chapter is the mathematics behind that description, keyed to the
implementation in `physicsnemo/experimental/nn/mesh_attention/`
(`attention.py`, `block.py`, `model.py`, `kernel_decoder.py`): the exact
form of each layer, the contracts each one guarantees, the one limitation
we can prove, and the decoder that removes it. Read @sec-architecture
first; nothing here redefines what a polar vector or an irrep is — it
uses them.

One paragraph of lineage. The stack generalizes **GLOBE** (arXiv
[2511.15856](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.15856)), a boundary-element
surrogate for boundary-driven PDEs. What is kept: the equivariance
structure of @sec-pde-theory (learned maps see only joint invariants of
relative displacement, normals, and boundary vector data), all-to-all
boundary information flow under quadrature weighting, and rigorous
nondimensionalization. What is replaced: GLOBE's bespoke kernel MLPs and
hand-assembled multiscale components give way to standard attention
blocks, residual streams, and typed projections — mainstream transformer
parts, with the contracts kept exact.

## Typed state and typed projections

All latent state lives in a `ScalarVectorState`: invariant-scalar
channels of shape $(N, C_s)$ and polar-vector channels of shape
$(N, C_v, D)$. These are the two irreps of @sec-typed-channels, and they
are the *only* representable types — pseudoscalars, axial vectors, and
higher-order tensors are rejected at construction time rather than
implicitly flattened into channels.

`TypedProjection` implements the allowed combination rules and nothing
else:

- scalar outputs are a learned linear map of the input scalars *plus the
  Gram invariants* $v_a \cdot v_b$ of the vector channels (the dot
  product is how vector information reaches scalar channels);
- vector outputs mix vector *channels* only, one coefficient per channel
  pair, applied identically to every Cartesian component:
  $v^{\text{out}}_{o} = \sum_c W_{oc}\, v_c$.

Because no learned layer ever sees a raw Cartesian component, absolute
coordinate, positional encoding, or vertex index, equivariance holds by
construction for any weights. `GeometryConditionedLinear` adds the two
elementary geometry-mediated type conversions — field-vector $\cdot$
geometry-vector $\to$ scalar, and field-scalar $\times$ geometry-vector
$\to$ vector — plus a dyad branch $\sum C\,(v\!\cdot\!g_a)\,g_b$ that
represents anisotropic maps like the normal projection $(v \cdot n)n$,
all while staying exactly linear in the field at fixed geometry.

Whether the vector channels *justify their cost* is an empirical question
with a measured answer: not essential on easy 2D geometry, essential on 3D and parametric problems — and it is oriented
transport, not raw width (@sec-scalar-only; history in
@sec-notebook, iteration 14).

## Signed moment attention

The central layer, `MeshAttention`, is a **finite-rank separable signed
integral operator** — the precise form of the "boundary self-attention"
of @sec-attention-role. For head $h$, typed projections produce scalar
and vector query/key features $q^0_{ihr}, k^0_{jhr} \in \mathbb R$ and
$q^1_{ihrd}, k^1_{jhrd} \in \mathbb R^D$, and the pair coefficient is

$$
a_{ijh}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{R_0+DR_1}}
\Bigl(
\sum_{r=1}^{R_0} q^0_{ihr}k^0_{jhr}
+\sum_{r=1}^{R_1} q^1_{ihr}\!\cdot\! k^1_{jhr}
\Bigr).
$$

The three departures from textbook attention (@sec-attention-role) appear
here as absences: **no softmax** (boundary-integral kernels are signed),
**no distance envelope or cutoff** (elliptic problems are global,
@sec-global-flow), **no normalization** (it would break drive linearity).
The output at receiver $i$ is the quadrature-weighted sum
$o_{ihf} = \sum_j \omega_j\, a_{ijh}\, v_{jhf}$, values retaining their
scalar/vector type.

Separability is what makes encode $O(N_s)$: the all-pairs sum
reassociates exactly into four typed **source moments**,

$$
M^{00}_{hrf}=\sum_j\omega_j k^0_{jhr}v^0_{jhf},\quad
M^{10}_{hrdf}=\sum_j\omega_j k^1_{jhrd}v^0_{jhf},\quad
M^{01}_{hrfe}=\sum_j\omega_j k^0_{jhr}v^1_{jhfe},\quad
M^{11}_{hrdfe}=\sum_j\omega_j k^1_{jhrd}v^1_{jhfe},
$$

built once and contracted at each receiver:

$$
o^0_{ihf}=\sum_r q^0_{ihr}M^{00}_{hrf}+\sum_{r,d}q^1_{ihrd}M^{10}_{hrdf},
\qquad
o^1_{ihfe}=\sum_r q^0_{ihr}M^{01}_{hrfe}+\sum_{r,d}q^1_{ihrd}M^{11}_{hrdfe}.
$$

This is an algebraic rearrangement, not an approximation: every source
contributes to every moment, every receiver reads every moment. A dense
`forward_reference` oracle evaluates the identical operator in
$O(N_sN_q)$ and backs value- and gradient-equality tests. In code the
four moments are typed views of one packed joint moment per head, built
by a single mesh-native `integrate_moment` call.

The price of separability, stated up front: per head, the effective score
matrix has rank at most $R_0 + DR_1$. One layer cannot represent an
arbitrary full-rank pair kernel, a pair-specific radial function, or a
singular Green kernel. Heads and ranks are capacity knobs, not physics.
This price is exactly what @sec-ceiling turns into a theorem.

## Two streams and the linearity contract

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: >
%%|   MeshTransformer dataflow as implemented in model.py. Encode (top) runs
%%|   once per boundary in O(N_s); decode (bottom) runs per query mesh in
%%|   O(N_q) per moment read, reusing the cached encoding. Blue boxes are
%%|   data, cream boxes are computation, green is the output.
flowchart TB
    classDef stage fill:#fff8e8,stroke:#8a6d1a,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef data fill:#eef4ff,stroke:#2a4a8a,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef out fill:#eaf7ea,stroke:#2a6a2a,color:#1a1a1a

    subgraph ENC["encode(domain) — O(N_s)"]
        DM["DomainMesh boundaries<br/>(cells: centroid, measure, normal)"]:::data --> QU["merge + cell quadrature<br/>center c, reference length L"]:::stage
        QU --> LIFT["operator lift (TypedProjection)<br/>fields + z_j + n_j + BC one-hot"]:::stage
        LIFT --> OB["MeshOperatorBlock × L_o<br/>typed RMS norm → moment attention → FFN<br/>(nonlinearities allowed here)"]:::stage
        DR["drive fields<br/>(boundary + global)"]:::data --> DLIFT["drive lift (GeometryConditionedLinear)<br/>linear in drive at fixed operator state"]:::stage
        OB --> DLIFT
        DLIFT --> DB["field blocks × L_d<br/>Linear- or NonlinearZero-MeshFieldBlock"]:::stage
        OB --> DB
        DB --> EB["EncodedBoundary<br/>(states, c, L, cached moments)"]:::data
    end
    subgraph DEC["decode(encoded, query_mesh)"]
        QP["query points"]:::data --> QB["query field blocks<br/>(moment or kernel decoder)"]:::stage
        EB --> QB
        QB --> OUT["typed output projection<br/>(bias-free)"]:::stage
        OUT --> PM["prediction at queries"]:::out
    end
```

Input fields carry one of two **roles**, and the two roles flow through
different streams:

- **Operator stream** (geometry, material data, PDE coefficients): source
  tokens pass through `MeshOperatorBlock`s — typed RMS norm, moment
  self-attention, equivariant feed-forward, LayerScale residuals. Biases
  and nonlinearities are *allowed* here: this stream describes the
  operator, not the solution amplitude.
- **Drive stream** (the boundary/global data the solution depends on): in
  `linear` mode (`LinearMeshFieldBlock`), attention queries and keys read
  *only* the operator state, values are bias-free linear in the drive,
  and the pointwise map is `GeometryConditionedLinear` — so the complete
  drive-to-output map satisfies $\mathcal N_\Gamma(0)=0$ and exact
  superposition at fixed geometry, to floating point.
  `quadratic` mode (`QuadraticFieldReadIn`) keeps the linear path
  and adds exactly one bilinear typed composition at the query read-in,
  making the output an exact degree-$\le 2$ polynomial in the drive for
  any weights — the *declared-degree* contract (@sec-nonlinear-fragility).
  `zero_preserving_nonlinear` mode (`NonlinearZeroMeshFieldBlock`) lets
  keys and values read the field through structurally multiplicative
  updates: zero-preservation remains exact, superposition intentionally does
  not.

The modes are **different Python classes**, not flags on one class,
so a future normalization or bias added to the nonlinear block cannot
invalidate the linear-mode (or declared-degree) proof unnoticed.

`encode` returns an `EncodedBoundary` — dimensionless source mesh,
operator and drive states, center, reference length, cached moments.
`decode` evaluates it at any query mesh; query points never interact,
and prediction at a point is independent of which other points are
requested — the reusability structure the Green representation
(@eq-green) suggests.

## The proved limitation: an angular ceiling at order two {#sec-ceiling}

At an ordinary interior query, the *only* query-side vector is the
centered position $x$ (the query normal is zeroed; no physical global
vector exists in the benchmark). Since the stack carries only scalars and
polar vectors, in `linear` mode with scalar output the moment decoder can
produce only

$$
u(x) = c(|x|^2) + b(|x|^2)\cdot x + x^\mathsf{T} A(|x|^2)\, x,
$$

because every additional pairing of $x$ with itself reduces to powers of
$|x|^2$. On any circle centered at the model origin, the angular content
is limited to Fourier orders $m \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ — one monopole, two
dipoles, two quadrupoles; a boundary-to-ring operator of rank at most
five. Width, heads, separable rank, and depth add channel multiplicity
and radial structure but **cannot create an $m \ge 3$ irrep**. This is a
representation nullspace — proved in the module documentation (§6.2),
confirmed by randomized-weight scans — and the checked-in benchmark
measures exactly it:

```{python}
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Pure-mode relative L2 response by boundary harmonic mode (checked-in
#|   reference_2026-07-01.json, 1,000 updates, 3 seeds, mode probes on 8
#|   geometries). The trained MeshTransformer transmits modes 0-2 and is at
#|   ~0.98-1.0 relative error (i.e., no response) for every mode >= 3 --
#|   the proved ceiling, not an optimization artifact. The dense invariant
#|   pair kernel, which forms joint source-query geometry, degrades smoothly
#|   instead.
import json
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

reference = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "reference_2026-07-01.json"))
responses = reference["pure_mode_relative_l2"]
modes = [str(m) for m in range(9)]
mt = [responses["mesh_transformer"][m] for m in modes]
pk = [responses["invariant_pair_kernel"][m] for m in modes]

x = np.arange(len(modes))
width = 0.38
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 3.4))
ax.bar(x - width / 2, mt, width, color="#2a78d6", label="MeshTransformer (135,945 p)")
ax.bar(x + width / 2, pk, width, color="#eda100", label="dense pair kernel (19,008 p)")
ax.axhline(1.0, color="#0b0b0b", lw=1.0, ls="--")
ax.text(8.42, 1.02, "no response", fontsize=8, color="#0b0b0b",
        ha="right", va="bottom")
ax.axvspan(2.5, 8.5, color="#e34948", alpha=0.06, lw=0)
ax.text(5.5, 1.14, "proved $m\\geq 3$ nullspace (linear mode, scalar output)",
        ha="center", fontsize=8.5, color="#52514e")
ax.set_xticks(x, [f"m={m}" for m in modes])
ax.set_xlabel("boundary harmonic mode (modes 1-4 occur in training)")
ax.set_ylabel("pure-mode relative $L^2$")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.24)
ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e1e0d9", lw=0.8)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 1.0))
for spine in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Two facts sharpen the diagnosis. Objective controls cannot fix it:
equal-interior-energy and uniform-pure-mode training leave mode-3/4
errors at $\approx$0.985 — you cannot optimize your way out of a
nullspace. And the two-by-two factorial locates the bottleneck in the
**source–query factorization**, not the boundary encoder: swapping the
moment decoder for a dense relative pair decoder improves ID error by
0.34–0.39, while adding the global encoder to the moment decoder changes
it by 0.00026. Once joint source–query geometry exists, the encoder helps
(23.7% on the pair model) — a division of labor @sec-parametric makes
precise.

## The fix: a kernel-basis query decoder {#sec-kernel-decoder}

The ceiling is a query-side representation nullspace induced by
separability, so the repair changes what the decoder *is*, not how it is
trained. `MeshTransformer(query_decoder="kernel")` (`kernel_decoder.py`)
replaces the separable moment contraction in the query field blocks with
a **dense, operator-conditioned pair-kernel dictionary** — the
plain-language version is @sec-decoder-role:

$$
u_{hf}(x) = \sum_j \kappa_h(x, y_j)\, V_{jhf},
\qquad
\kappa_h(x, y_j) = \sum_m C_{mh}(\mathrm{op}_j)\, \varphi_m(x, y_j),
$$

evaluated densely over query–source pairs at the documented price of
$O(N_qN_s)$ per decode (chunked — a pure memory control that never
changes the operator; a hierarchical/FMM backend would be a separate
numerical backend converging to this dense oracle). Each ingredient is a
lesson the program paid for earlier:

- **Exact-quadrature singular members — the H1d lesson (@sec-ladder).**
  The singular members are *exact* integrals of the free-space kernels
  over each boundary cell, dimension-dispatched: for the double layer,
  the signed subtended angle over 2D segments and the van
  Oosterom–Strackee signed solid angle over 3D triangles (entries at an
  interior point of a closed boundary sum to exactly $-1$); for the
  single layer, the Hess–Smith closed form in 2D and a per-edge
  $\operatorname{asinh}$ form in 3D. H1d showed that exactly singular
  kernels *lose* under midpoint quadrature — the optimizer mollifies the
  near field at the cost of operator fidelity — so the closed forms are
  essential, validated to $\sim 10^{-14}$.
- **Operator-conditioned coefficients — the conditioning role the
  parametric study licenses (@sec-parametric).** The $C_{mh}$ are a linear map of each source
  token's operator-state invariants (scalars plus vector Gram
  invariants): the globally encoded boundary conditions the kernel. That
  is exactly the encoder role the evidence licenses — conditioning
  coefficients of a fixed dictionary, with the dictionary, not the
  conditioner, carrying the angular and radial structure.
- **A dense pair kernel — the factorial finding (above).** The
  bottleneck was the source–query factorization; any pair kernel
  lifts the ceiling, and the subtended-angle member alone carries every
  angular order.

The contracts survive intact. The two linearity classes are again
separate Python classes (the linear decoder's kernel reads only operator
state; the nonlinear-zero class lets the kernel read drive invariants
while values stay bias-free). All pair features are joint O($D$)
invariants of $\{x-y,\ n_y,\ \text{source-state vectors}\}$. Query
independence is *bitwise*: the dense evaluation avoids
batch-shape-dependent reductions on the query axis, so decoding a query
subset reproduces the corresponding rows of the full batch exactly.

The spectral fix is documented in the test suite, not just claimed: a
paired random-weight ring test (`test_kernel_decoder.py`) asserts on the
same seeds that the moment decoder's $m \ge 3$ ring content is
$\le 2\times10^{-11}$ (the ceiling) while the kernel decoder's is
$\ge 10^{-6}$ (lifted); the module's contract tests are parametrized over
both decoders.

On the frozen 64-case reference bank, three seeds, 3,000 updates:

| model (reference bank, 3,000 updates, 3 seeds) | params | ID | freq-OOD | mode-6 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| kernel decoder, full dictionary | 110,561 | 0.0399 ± 0.0035 | 0.487 ± 0.047 | 0.48 |
| **kernel decoder, dictionary-only** (`kernel_mlp_members=0`) | 105,089 | 0.0409 ± 0.0076 | **0.0713 ± 0.0008** | 0.064 |
| moment decoder (reference capacity) | 135,945 | 0.4503 ± 0.0016 | 1.000 | 1.00 |
| free-form pair kernel (control) | 19,008 | 0.0398 ± 0.0013 | 0.497 | 0.41 |

: Three-seed confirmation on the frozen 64-case reference bank —
fixed-compute discipline, 3,000 updates for every row (which is why the
free-form pair kernel reads 0.0398 here rather than its checked-in
1,000-update 0.107). Checked-in artifact. {#tbl-kernel-refbank}

The repair holds where it counts: the kernel decoder cuts the moment
decoder's ID error 11.3$\times$ (0.4503 $\to$ 0.0399) and the ceiling
stays gone at three seeds. (The single-seed gate that preceded this
table, and its mode-response figure, are in the notebook —
@sec-notebook, iteration 7.)

## Dictionary selection {#sec-dictionary-selection}

The freq-OOD column of @tbl-kernel-refbank contains the finding that the
rest of the dictionary program turns on. The full dictionary's freq-OOD
*degrades with training* (0.12 at 1,000 updates $\to$ 0.487 at 3,000)
while the dictionary-only ablation holds 0.0713 at identical ID. The
mechanism: the near-zero-initialized smooth MLP members grow during
training to absorb residual ID error, sliding the kernel toward
value-interpolator behavior on unseen frequencies. **Training trades
structure for interpolation** — the data does not select the structured
members; selection has to be imposed.

That finding was then tested on every suite in the program — nonlinear
Liouville, screened Laplace, 3D Laplace, and finally a pre-registered
four-arm 2D ablation and its 3D disentangler. Two working hypotheses were
refuted along the way (the full chronology is in notebook iterations 8–13,
@sec-notebook). One rule remained consistent across every suite:

> **The dictionary carries the singularity; conditioning carries the
> smoothness; nonlinearity needs a smooth basis.** In drive-linear
> operation the dictionary is the exact singular member(s) alone, and
> operator conditioning carries all smoothness — best-in-class on 2D
> Laplace, screened Laplace, and 3D Laplace. In nonlinear field mode the
> polynomial members are essential. MLP members are prunable
> everywhere.

This is the member-level instance of a rule the program established
twice before at smaller scales: the parametric study proved the
coefficient-level version (conditioning interpolates; only built-in
structure extrapolates, @sec-parametric), and the pruning study the
parameter-level version (free capacity is not neutral; pruning it is
lossless or better, @sec-learned-bie). The twist at architecture scale: the unstructured
capacity does not train toward zero — it actively grows to eat ID error.
Current-best evidence tables: @sec-dictionary-ablation,
@sec-dictionary-3d, @sec-singonly-universality, @sec-single-layer.

## What the layer is, and is not

The scope used throughout the rest of the book: `MeshAttention`
is an exact, similarity-covariant, quadrature-weighted, low-order
**global moment primitive** with linear cost and a dense oracle — a
rigorous building block for boundary functionals. It is *not* a general
elliptic surrogate: its separable finite-rank kernel cannot represent
the singular, domain-dependent Poisson kernel, and its default moment
query decoder has the exact $m\le2$ ceiling — lifted, at the documented
$O(N_qN_s)$ price and confirmed on three seeds on the reference bank
(@tbl-kernel-refbank), by the kernel-basis decoder of
@sec-kernel-decoder. With the moment decoder it reaches ID
$0.458\pm0.002$ on the reference bank where a 19k-parameter dense
invariant pair kernel reaches $0.107\pm0.025$ (the checked-in
1,000-update protocol; @tbl-kernel-refbank reports the same pair at
3,000 updates) — and @sec-learned-bie
shows that 3 parameters beat both, once the decoder respects the PDE.
(That comparison exists because the benchmark's PDE is known; under the
product scope it is the oracle the general architecture is measured
against, not a design it can adopt.)
